listeningParts.title: Joining a volcano hiking trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a tour company to book a guided hike on a volcano.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Fire Mountain Tours, this is Callum. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm on holiday here next month with my husband, and we'd love to do one of your volcano hikes. Could you tell me what you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Certainly. We have three main trips. The easiest is the Lava Fields Walk. It takes about three hours and goes across old lava flows at the bottom of the mountain. There's not much climbing, so it's suitable for almost anyone, including children over eight.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Okay. And the others?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The second is the Crater Rim Hike, which is our most popular. You drive up to the car park at fifteen hundred metres, and then walk up to the edge of the main crater and around it. It takes around six hours in total, and you need to be reasonably fit, because the path is steep in places and the ground is loose.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And the third one?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's the Summit Sunrise trip. You start at two in the morning and climb to the summit in the dark, so that you reach the top at sunrise. It's spectacular, but it's very demanding: around nine hours of walking, and the summit is at over three thousand metres, so some people feel the effects of the altitude.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think the Crater Rim Hike sounds about right for us. We walk quite a lot at home, but we're not experienced mountaineers.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good choice. That trip runs every day except Sunday. Which date were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Could we do the nineteenth?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The nineteenth is a Wednesday. Yes, there are places available. The price is eighty-five euros per person. That includes transport from your hotel, the guide, a helmet, and a packed lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: A helmet? Is it dangerous?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a precaution. The volcano is active, and occasionally small stones are thrown out of the crater. Our guides check the activity reports every morning with the volcano observatory, and if the risk is too high, we change the route or cancel the trip. If we cancel, you get a full refund, or you can move to another day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. What should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Proper walking boots are essential; we won't allow anyone to join in trainers or sandals, because the volcanic rock is very sharp. You'll also need a waterproof jacket and a warm layer. Even in summer, it can be cold and windy near the crater. And bring at least two litres of water per person, sun cream and sunglasses.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: We don't have walking boots with us. Can we hire them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, we hire boots for ten euros a pair. Just tell me your shoe sizes when you book, so we can have them ready.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Great. And what time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The minibus picks people up between seven and seven thirty, depending on where your hotel is. Where are you staying?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The Hotel Miramar, on the seafront.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's one of our first pick-ups, so it'll be seven o'clock, outside the main entrance. Could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Laura Fairbanks. F-A-I-R-B-A-N-K-S.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know about your health, for example heart or breathing problems?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No, we're both fine. Although my husband is allergic to nuts, if that matters for the lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It does, thank you. I'll make a note so the kitchen prepares a nut-free lunch for him. To confirm the booking, we need a deposit of thirty euros per person, which you can pay online using the link I'll send you by email. The rest is paid in cash or by card to the guide on the day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Perfect. One last question: will we actually see lava?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'm afraid I can't promise that. Sometimes, if there's been recent activity, you can see a red glow inside the crater, but most of the time you'll see steam and smoke, and smell the sulphur. It's still very impressive, though, and the views across the island are amazing.

listeningParts.title: Earthquake preparedness at work
listeningParts.contextDescription: A safety officer speaks to new staff at an office about what to do in an earthquake.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Harbourview Engineering. I'm Nadia, the health and safety officer, and this morning I want to talk to you about earthquakes. As you probably know, this city lies close to a major fault line, and scientists estimate there's a significant chance of a damaging earthquake here in the next fifty years. So it's important that everyone knows exactly what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: First, the building itself. This office was built in 2012, and it was designed to meet the latest earthquake standards. It sits on special rubber bearings, which allow the building to move separately from the ground and reduce the shaking inside. That means it's very unlikely to collapse. However, people are often injured in earthquakes not because buildings fall down, but because objects inside them fall over or are thrown across the room. That's why all our bookcases and filing cabinets are fixed to the walls, and why we ask you not to keep heavy objects on high shelves.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Now, if you feel an earthquake, the rule is: drop, cover and hold on. Drop to your hands and knees before the shaking knocks you down. Take cover under a strong desk or table, protecting your head and neck. And hold on to it until the shaking stops. If there's no table nearby, crouch next to an inside wall, away from windows, and cover your head with your arms.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: What you should not do is run outside during the shaking. Many injuries happen when people are hit by falling glass or pieces of buildings as they leave. And please don't use the lifts, either during an earthquake or afterwards, because they may stop working or be damaged. Some people believe that standing in a doorway is the safest place, but in modern buildings, doorways are no stronger than other parts of the structure, so that advice is out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: When the shaking stops, wait for instructions from your floor warden. Each floor has two wardens, who wear orange jackets. If the building needs to be evacuated, they'll lead you down the stairs. Our assembly point is in the car park of the sports centre across the road, not the main car park behind this building, because that's next to a tall wall which could fall. At the assembly point, your manager will check that everyone from your team is there.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Be aware that a large earthquake is usually followed by aftershocks, which can continue for days or even weeks. Some can be strong enough to cause further damage, so be prepared to drop, cover and hold on again.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: We also keep emergency supplies in the building, in case staff are unable to get home, for example if roads or bridges are closed. There are emergency kits on every floor, in the cupboard next to the kitchen. Each one contains water, food bars, a first-aid kit, a torch and a radio that works without batteries, using a handle that you turn. We check the kits every six months and replace anything that's out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: We also strongly recommend that you prepare a small kit for your own home and agree a plan with your family, for example a place to meet if you're separated and a friend or relative outside the city that everyone can contact, since local phone networks are often overloaded after an earthquake. You'll find a checklist on the staff website.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Finally, we hold an earthquake drill twice a year, in April and October, and the whole building takes part. You'll hear a long, continuous alarm, which is different from the fire alarm, which goes on and off. Right, does anyone have any questions?

listeningParts.title: A field trip to study a volcano
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Hannah and Kofi, discuss a field trip with their lecturer.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Come in, Hannah, Kofi. So, now that you're back from the field trip to Tenerife, I'd like to hear how your research went before you start writing it up.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It went really well, thanks. As you know, our project was about how local people perceive the risk of a future eruption of Mount Teide, and whether they'd know what to do if one happened.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your data?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Mainly through face-to-face interviews. We interviewed eighty-six people in three towns at different distances from the volcano. We'd planned to do a hundred, but it took longer than we expected, because a lot of people wanted to talk for much longer than the fifteen minutes we'd planned.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's actually a good sign. People were interested in the topic, then?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Very. What surprised us most was that most people didn't think an eruption was likely in their lifetime, even though Teide is classified as active. Only about one in four thought there was a real chance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Partly because the last eruption on the island was in 1909, so nobody alive remembers one. Several people said things like, 'It's been quiet for over a hundred years, so why would it erupt now?' Volcanologists would say that's not how volcanoes work, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And there were also some interesting differences between groups. Older people were generally less worried than younger people, which we hadn't expected. We thought older residents might know more about the volcano's history.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Did you find any explanation for that?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: We think it might be linked to social media. Younger people said they'd seen news about earthquake swarms under the island in recent years, and some had been following the 2021 eruption on La Palma, the neighbouring island, very closely online.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's a very plausible connection. La Palma would have made the risk feel much more real. What about preparedness?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That was more worrying. Fewer than a third of people knew where their nearest evacuation route was, and almost nobody had an emergency bag ready. Most people said they'd simply wait for the authorities to tell them what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Which isn't unreasonable, as long as the warning systems work. Did you visit the monitoring centre?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, on the third day. That was one of the highlights. The scientists showed us how they measure small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground and the gases coming out of the volcano. They said changes in gas emissions are often one of the earliest signs that magma is moving.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: They also told us that the biggest challenge isn't detecting activity, but communicating it to the public without causing panic. If they warn too often and nothing happens, people stop listening.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's an important point for your discussion. It's sometimes called the 'cry wolf' effect. Did they say how they deal with it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They use a colour-coded alert system, from green to red, and they publish regular updates even when nothing is happening, so that people get used to trusting one source of information rather than rumours on social media.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sensible. Now, any problems with the fieldwork?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: The main one was language. Our Spanish isn't great, so we relied on a local student, Elena, to help with interviews. She was excellent, but sometimes we weren't sure whether her translations were exactly what people had said.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: You should mention that as a limitation. You could also record the interviews, with permission, and have a sample checked by another translator.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good idea. We did record about half of them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then do that. Right, I'd like your first draft by the end of the month, and please include a map showing the three towns.

listeningParts.title: Tsunamis
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an earth sciences course on the causes of tsunamis and how their effects can be reduced.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. In today's lecture, we're going to look at tsunamis: what causes them, why they're so destructive, and what can be done to reduce the number of people they kill.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The word tsunami comes from Japanese and means 'harbour wave', because fishermen would return to find their harbours destroyed, although they'd noticed nothing unusual out at sea. Tsunamis used to be called tidal waves, but that's misleading, because they have nothing to do with tides.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most tsunamis are caused by large earthquakes under the sea, particularly at subduction zones, where one of the Earth's plates is being pushed beneath another. Pressure builds up over hundreds of years, and when the plates suddenly slip, the sea floor can rise or fall by several metres. This moves the entire column of water above it, from the sea floor to the surface. Tsunamis can also be caused by underwater landslides, volcanic eruptions and, very rarely, by meteorites hitting the ocean.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A tsunami is very different from an ordinary wave. Ordinary waves are caused by wind and only affect the water near the surface. Tsunami waves involve the whole depth of the ocean, and they have an extremely long wavelength; the distance between one wave crest and the next can be over a hundred kilometres. In deep water, they travel as fast as a jet aircraft, at around eight hundred kilometres per hour, but they may be less than a metre high, so ships at sea often don't notice them at all.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: As the wave approaches the coast and the water becomes shallower, it slows down and grows much taller. Often, the first sign is not a wall of water but the sea suddenly drawing back, exposing the sea floor far beyond the normal low tide. Tragically, people sometimes walk out to look at the exposed beach, not realising that the wave will arrive within minutes. Another common misunderstanding is that a tsunami is a single wave. In fact, there's usually a series of waves, and the first is often not the largest.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The deadliest tsunami in recorded history occurred in the Indian Ocean on the twenty-sixth of December 2004, after an earthquake off the coast of Sumatra in Indonesia. It killed around two hundred and thirty thousand people in fourteen countries. One reason the death toll was so high was that, unlike the Pacific, the Indian Ocean had no warning system at the time. In some places, such as Sri Lanka and India, the waves arrived two hours after the earthquake, which would have been plenty of time to evacuate if people had been warned.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Since then, a warning system has been established in the Indian Ocean. Such systems rely on two main types of information. First, earthquake measurements, which show where and how strong an earthquake is. And second, sensors on the sea floor that detect changes in water pressure as a tsunami passes above them. These send signals to buoys on the surface, which transmit the data by satellite to warning centres.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But technology alone isn't enough. The 2011 tsunami in Japan showed this. Japan has the world's most advanced warning system and many coastal defences, including sea walls over ten metres high. Yet the waves were higher than expected and went over many of the walls, and around eighteen thousand people died. Studies afterwards found that some people didn't evacuate because they trusted the sea walls to protect them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So education is crucial. In some communities, traditional knowledge has saved lives. On the Indonesian island of Simeulue, very close to the 2004 earthquake, only seven people died out of around seventy-eight thousand, because people had passed down stories about an earlier tsunami in 1907, which taught them to run to high ground when the ground shook. Today, many coastal areas have signs showing evacuation routes, and schools carry out regular drills. Next week, we'll look at how coastal planning and natural barriers such as mangrove forests can also reduce the impact.

readingPassages.title: The year without a summer
paragraphs: In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, produced the largest eruption in recorded history. The explosions were heard more than two thousand kilometres away, and some people on nearby islands believed they were hearing the sound of cannons. Before the eruption, Tambora was over four thousand metres high; afterwards, about a third of the mountain had disappeared, leaving a crater six kilometres wide.

The immediate effects on the region were catastrophic. Clouds of hot gas, ash and rock, known as pyroclastic flows, rushed down the sides of the volcano at enormous speed, destroying villages and killing almost everyone in their path. Thick layers of ash covered fields across Sumbawa and the neighbouring island of Lombok, ruining crops and poisoning water supplies. Estimates vary, but it is thought that around ten thousand people died during the eruption itself, and that tens of thousands more died in the following months from starvation and disease.

The effects of the eruption, however, were not limited to Indonesia. Tambora blasted huge quantities of sulphur gas high into the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the level at which clouds and weather form. There, the gas combined with water to form tiny droplets, which spread around the globe and reflected part of the sun's energy back into space. Because there is no rain in the stratosphere to wash these particles out, they remained there for several years, causing average temperatures around the world to fall by around half a degree Celsius.

This may not sound like much, but the consequences in 1816 were dramatic. In parts of Europe and North America, it became known as 'the year without a summer'. In New England, in the north-eastern United States, snow fell in June, and frosts in July and August killed crops. In western Europe, it rained almost continuously throughout the summer, and harvests of wheat and potatoes failed. Food prices rose sharply, and there were riots in Britain, France and Switzerland. In Ireland, the cold, wet weather was followed by an epidemic of typhus, which killed tens of thousands of people.

The crisis had long-lasting social effects. In the United States, thousands of farmers left New England and moved west in search of better land, contributing to the settlement of states such as Ohio and Indiana. In Germany, the high price of oats, which were used to feed horses, may have encouraged the inventor Karl Drais to develop a 'running machine', an early form of bicycle that did not need to be fed, which he demonstrated in 1817. Although this connection is difficult to prove, it is often mentioned by historians of transport.

The gloomy summer also left a mark on culture. A group of young English writers, including Mary Shelley and Lord Byron, spent the summer of 1816 at a villa beside Lake Geneva in Switzerland. Kept indoors by the constant storms, they held a competition to see who could write the most frightening story. Mary Shelley's contribution later became the novel Frankenstein, published in 1818. Some art historians have also suggested that the vivid orange and red skies in paintings by the English artist J. M. W. Turner during this period reflect the volcanic particles in the atmosphere.

Remarkably, nobody at the time connected these events with the eruption on the other side of the world. News travelled slowly, and the idea that a volcano could affect the global climate had not yet been developed. It was not until the twentieth century that scientists, studying the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 and later ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica, which contain layers of sulphur from past eruptions, were able to show the link.

Today, Tambora's story is studied not only by historians but also by scientists and governments. It shows how vulnerable food systems can be to sudden changes in climate, and how a disaster in one part of the world can have consequences on the other side of it. Some researchers argue that an eruption of a similar size, which is likely to happen at some point in the next few centuries, could cause serious disruption to global food supplies, and that countries should plan for such an event.

readingPassages.title: Can earthquakes be predicted?
paragraphs: Of all natural disasters, earthquakes are among the most frightening, partly because they strike without warning. Hurricanes can be tracked for days as they cross the ocean, and floods can often be forecast from rainfall, but an earthquake can destroy a city in less than a minute. For more than a century, scientists have searched for a reliable way of predicting when and where earthquakes will occur. So far, despite enormous effort, they have not succeeded.

To understand why, it helps to know what causes earthquakes. The Earth's outer layer is broken into large plates, which move slowly, at roughly the speed at which fingernails grow. Where plates meet, they often become locked together along faults, and stress builds up in the surrounding rock. Eventually, the stress becomes greater than the strength of the rock, and the fault suddenly slips, releasing energy in the form of seismic waves. The difficulty is that scientists cannot directly observe conditions deep underground, where most earthquakes begin, and small differences in the properties of rocks can determine whether a fault slips today or in a hundred years.

Throughout history, people have reported strange events before earthquakes. Animals are said to behave unusually, water levels in wells rise or fall, and lights have been seen in the sky. Some of these reports may reflect real physical changes, but most are collected only after an earthquake has happened, when people are searching for explanations. Scientific studies have generally failed to find signals that occur consistently before earthquakes and rarely at other times, which is what a useful prediction method requires.

There has been one famous apparent success. In February 1975, Chinese authorities ordered the evacuation of the city of Haicheng after a series of small earthquakes, changes in groundwater and reports of unusual animal behaviour. The next day, a powerful earthquake struck, destroying much of the city. Thousands of lives were probably saved. However, the following year, an even larger earthquake hit the city of Tangshan without any warning, killing at least two hundred and forty thousand people. Most scientists now believe that Haicheng was a lucky case, made possible by an unusually long sequence of small earthquakes beforehand.

Prediction attempts have also had serious consequences when they failed. In 2009, a series of small earthquakes worried residents of the Italian city of L'Aquila. At a meeting, experts concluded that a major earthquake was unlikely, and an official reassured the public. Days later, an earthquake killed more than three hundred people. Six scientists and an official were convicted of manslaughter for giving misleading information, though the scientists' convictions were later overturned on appeal. The case alarmed researchers around the world, who feared that scientists would become reluctant to give advice.

Instead of predicting individual earthquakes, seismologists now concentrate on forecasting, which means estimating the probability of earthquakes in a particular area over a period of years or decades. These forecasts are based on the history of past earthquakes, the rate at which plates are moving and measurements of how the ground is deforming. In California, for example, scientists estimate that there is a greater than ninety-five per cent chance of an earthquake of magnitude 6.7 or larger in the next thirty years. Such forecasts cannot tell people when to leave their homes, but they are extremely useful for setting building standards and planning insurance.

A further approach is early warning. When an earthquake begins, it produces two main types of waves: faster primary waves, which cause relatively little damage, and slower secondary waves, which cause most of the shaking. Networks of sensors can detect the primary waves and send an alert electronically, which travels much faster than the seismic waves themselves. Depending on the distance from the earthquake, this can give people between a few seconds and about a minute of warning. Japan, Mexico and parts of the United States already have such systems, which can automatically stop trains, open fire station doors and send alerts to mobile phones.

A few seconds may not sound like much, but it can be enough for people to take cover under a table, for surgeons to stop operating and for trains to slow down. Researchers are also experimenting with using the sensors already built into smartphones to detect earthquakes in countries that cannot afford expensive networks. While the dream of predicting earthquakes may never be realised, these more modest goals are already saving lives.

readingPassages.title: There is no such thing as a natural disaster
paragraphs: Earthquakes, floods, hurricanes and droughts are usually described as natural disasters. The phrase seems obvious: these events are caused by forces of nature rather than by human action. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that the term is misleading, and even harmful. A hazard, they point out, is a natural event; a disaster is what happens when that hazard meets a population that is unable to cope with it. Whether a hazard becomes a disaster, and how severe that disaster is, depends largely on human decisions.

This argument was popularised in the 1970s by a group of geographers, including Phil O'Keefe, Ken Westgate and Ben Wisner, whose article 'Taking the naturalness out of natural disasters' became highly influential. They noted that, while the number of hazards was not obviously increasing, the number of people killed and affected by disasters was rising rapidly, particularly in poorer countries. The explanation, they argued, lay not in nature but in the vulnerability of the people exposed to hazards, which was itself the result of poverty, inequality and poor planning.

Comparisons between countries illustrate the point clearly. In January 2010, an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 struck near Port-au-Prince, the capital of Haiti, killing somewhere between one hundred thousand and three hundred thousand people. A month later, an earthquake in Chile released around five hundred times more energy, yet it killed fewer than six hundred people. The difference was not mainly due to geology. Chile had strict building codes, which were generally enforced, and a long experience of earthquakes, whereas in Haiti many buildings were constructed cheaply without reinforcement, and the government lacked the resources to enforce standards.

Vulnerability also varies within countries. When Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans in 2005, the areas that flooded most severely were largely low-lying neighbourhoods where poorer residents lived. Many of them did not own cars and could not leave the city when an evacuation was ordered. Similarly, during the European heatwave of 2003, which killed around seventy thousand people, the victims were disproportionately elderly people living alone, often in apartments without air conditioning, who had little contact with neighbours or relatives. In each case, social factors determined who lived and who died.

Human activity can also increase the hazards themselves. Draining wetlands and cutting down forests can make floods more frequent and severe, because the land is less able to absorb rainfall. Building on unstable slopes increases the risk of landslides. Extracting large quantities of groundwater has caused parts of cities such as Jakarta and Mexico City to sink, sometimes by more than twenty centimetres a year, making them more vulnerable to flooding. And climate change, driven by human emissions of greenhouse gases, is making some hazards, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall, more intense.

Critics of the 'no natural disasters' argument accept much of this, but they warn against taking it too far. Some events are so extreme that no society could fully protect itself against them; the 2011 tsunami in Japan, a wealthy and well-prepared country, still killed around eighteen thousand people. Others worry that the phrase may be used to blame governments or communities unfairly, or that it may distract attention from the need to understand the natural processes involved. Seismologists and meteorologists, they point out, remain essential to reducing disaster risk.

Nevertheless, the change in thinking has influenced international policy. The Sendai Framework, agreed by United Nations member states in 2015, emphasises reducing risk before disasters occur rather than simply responding afterwards. It encourages governments to invest in safer buildings and infrastructure, early warning systems and land-use planning, and to ensure that the poorest and most vulnerable groups are included in decision-making. Research by the World Bank suggests that every dollar spent on making infrastructure more resilient can save around four dollars in future losses.

In my view, the most important contribution of this way of thinking is that it replaces fatalism with responsibility. If disasters are simply acts of nature, there is little that can be done except to respond when they happen. If, on the other hand, they are the product of choices about where and how we build, who is protected and who is left exposed, then they can be prevented, or at least made far less deadly. The language we use, it turns out, matters a great deal.
